## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The telephone CBT trial excluded possible dementia or marked cognitive impairment (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score <21), active suicidal plans or intent, unstable serious illness, and primary psychotic, bipolar, or substance-use disorder; its results therefore do not establish efficacy for these excluded groups. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] In a randomized trial of 72 people with PD and depression, a 10-session telephone CBT intervention added to usual care improved Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores by 6.53 points versus −0.27 with usual care; benefits persisted during six-month follow-up that included monthly CBT contacts. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Mindfulness-based yoga and meditation trials in mild-to-moderate PD suggest benefits for depressive symptoms compared with stretching and resistance exercise, but these programs and selected trial populations differ, so a single effect size should not be generalized across them. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6583059/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9862216/
- [statement] The mindfulness-yoga trial reported greater anxiety, depression and health-related quality-of-life improvement than stretching/resistance exercise, with similar physical benefits. Yoga classes lasted 90 minutes versus 60 minutes for controls. Unblinded participants, convenience sampling and exclusion of severe motor limitations restrict attribution and generalization. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6583059/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In a 136-person trial, eight weeks of computerized cognitive training did not improve the primary planning-accuracy outcome or subjective cognitive complaints compared with an active control. A secondary processing-speed improvement had limited clinical impact, and no group differences remained at six months. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] At one- and two-year COGTIPS follow-up, cognitive training showed no advantage on neuropsychological outcomes or conversion of cognitive status compared with an active control. Missing assessments, particularly during COVID-19 restrictions, limit interpretation. The result concerns the studied eight-week program. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10724826/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] PD-adapted CBT can improve depressive and anxiety symptoms compared with usual care or other control conditions; trial effects should not be interpreted as proof that every patient benefits. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447579/
- [statement] The Cochrane review summary reported seven studies and 225 participants with PD-related mild cognitive impairment or dementia: it found no evidence of global-cognition improvement, and apparent attention/verbal-memory benefits did not survive sensitivity analysis. Evidence certainty was low, so this is uncertainty about efficacy rather than proof of ineffectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33780379/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD

## Facts and statements

- [statement] PD-adapted CBT uses cognitive and behavioral coping skills. Depression protocols include behavioral activation, cognitive restructuring and anxiety management; anxiety protocols include psychoeducation, exposure, thought restructuring and home practice. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9290129/
- [statement] In Moonen and colleagues’ 48-person anxiety trial, ten weekly CBT sessions did not significantly outperform clinical monitoring on the primary Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. The secondary Parkinson Anxiety Scale favored CBT, so outcome choice materially affects interpretation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9290129/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Gwak and Park’s 2026 anxiety meta-analysis reported a pooled benefit for psychological and mind–body interventions but rated overall evidence certainty very low. The prediction interval included no effect, and most comparisons used inactive controls. The mindfulness/mind–body subgroup interval included no effect; subgroup differences were not statistically established. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13685121/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] The PD-MCI group-training trial randomized 64 participants to six weeks of multidomain training or low-intensity physical activity; phonemic fluency improved significantly, but the overall executive-function interaction was only a statistical trend. The authors called for longitudinal studies before inferring slower cognitive decline. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721510/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Selected short-term cognitive-test gains should not be presented as proof of dementia prevention: the PD-MCI group-training study called for longitudinal testing, whereas COGTIPS found no long-term cognitive or cognitive-status conversion advantage. The studies used different populations and training protocols. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721510/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10724826/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/
- [statement] The 2025 CBT meta-analysis included 16 RCTs and 682 participants, with searches updated through February 29, 2024; it found pooled improvements in depression and anxiety but no statistically significant pooled quality-of-life improvement. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447579/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In the mindfulness-yoga trial, 138 participants received eight weeks of yoga or stretching/resistance exercise; the yoga program reduced anxiety and depressive symptoms and improved health-related quality of life, while motor dysfunction and mobility benefits were described as comparable to exercise. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6583059/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In the 68-participant mindfulness-meditation trial, both meditation and exercise groups improved on cognitive performance immediately after treatment; meditation was not shown to provide a superior cognitive benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9862216/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Cognitive-training findings in PD are task-specific and inconsistent: one PD-MCI trial favored training on phonemic fluency, whereas a larger computerized-training trial found no benefit on its primary planning-accuracy outcome and no group differences at follow-up. These results do not establish broad or durable cognitive improvement. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721510/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/
- [statement] A stress-and-mindfulness viewpoint presented potential effects on PD progression as a hypothetical mechanistic framework informed partly by animal studies; this source does not demonstrate that mindfulness slows human PD progression. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894549/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Apparent treatment benefits need interpretation against control design and outcome choice: the telephone CBT investigators could not fully separate psychotherapy-specific effects from contact and attention, and the computerized cognitive-training investigators found only minor secondary gains with limited clinical impact despite a null primary outcome. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/

## Research summary — CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD

PD-adapted CBT addresses mood and anxiety through cognitive and behavioral coping skills. A randomized trial supports telephone CBT added to usual care for depression, while an anxiety trial had different results on its primary and PD-specific secondary measures. Mindfulness yoga and meditation trials suggest mood benefits in selected people with mild-to-moderate PD, but broader anxiety evidence has very low certainty. Cognitive training targets cognitive performance: selected short-term test gains coexist with negative primary and long-term trial outcomes. These studies do not establish dementia prevention. Findings depend on population, comparator, training format and outcome measure.
